blocks.text: Sorting is one of the first real algorithms every engineer learns, and most of the famous ones share a single idea: they decide the order by comparing elements two at a time.
Is this one bigger than that one? Swap them if needed. Repeat in a clever way until everything is in order. That entire family is called comparison based sorting.
If the only thing your sort does to work out the order is ask "is a less than b?", then it is a comparison based sort.

content.title: 1. What Makes a Sort Comparison Based

blocks.text: A comparison based sort never looks inside a value. It only asks how two elements relate to each other. That is both its great strength and its hard limit.

items: Strength: it works on anything you can order, including numbers, strings, dates, and custom objects with a compare function.
Limit: because it only ever compares, there is a floor on how fast it can possibly be.

blocks.text: That floor is O(n log n). No comparison based sort can beat it in the worst case. The reason is just counting: with n elements there are n factorial possible orderings, and each comparison only splits the remaining possibilities in two. You need about n log n comparisons to narrow it down to the one correct order.
O(n log n) is the speed limit for comparison sorting. To go faster you must stop comparing and start using the values themselves, which is exactly what non comparison sorts do.
Merge Sort is the cleanest example of this family and the one interviewers love most. It is built on divide and conquer.

items: Divide: split the array into two halves.
Conquer: sort each half by calling merge sort on it again.
Combine: merge the two sorted halves back into one sorted array.

blocks.text: The real work happens in the merge step. Because both halves are already sorted, you walk them with two pointers and always take the smaller front element.

codes.python:
def merge_sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr

    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])    # sort the left half
    right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])   # sort the right half
    return merge(left, right)       # combine two sorted halves

def merge(left, right):
    result = []
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:     # <= keeps the sort stable
            result.append(left[i]); i += 1
        else:
            result.append(right[j]); j += 1
    result.extend(left[i:])
    result.extend(right[j:])
    return result

blocks.text: The <= in the merge is not an accident. Taking the left element on ties is what keeps Merge Sort stable, so equal items keep their original order.

content.title: 3. Why Merge Sort is O(n log n)

blocks.text: Two small questions explain the speed.
How many levels?
Each level splits every piece in half, so it takes about log n splits to reach pieces of size one.
How much work per level?
Merging all the pieces at one level touches every element exactly once, which is O(n) work.
Multiply them together: log n levels times O(n) work each gives O(n log n), every single time, in the best case and the worst case alike.
Not every comparison sort is fancy. The two simplest ones are worth knowing because they show the idea in its rawest form.
Insertion Sort
Walk left to right and insert each element into its correct spot among the ones already sorted behind it, exactly the way most people sort a hand of playing cards.
It is O(n^2) in general, but O(n) when the array is already nearly sorted, which makes it surprisingly handy for small or almost ordered data.
Bubble Sort
Repeatedly swap neighbouring elements that are out of order, so the largest value bubbles to the end on each pass. It is mostly a teaching tool and is rarely the right choice in real code.
Insertion and Bubble Sort are O(n^2). Fine for tiny inputs, painful for large ones. Reach for Merge Sort once the data grows.
When you choose a sort, two properties matter almost as much as speed.

items: Stable: equal elements keep their original relative order. This matters when you sort by one key and then another.
In place: it sorts using almost no extra memory.

blocks.text: Comparison based sorting is your safe default. Reach for it when:

items: Your data is not just small integers in a known range
You need to sort strings, objects, or anything with a custom order
You want a reliable O(n log n) sort that works everywhere

blocks.text: If your data is a pile of bounded integers, a non comparison sort can actually beat the O(n log n) limit. We cover those in the non comparison lesson.
Most standard library sort functions are comparison based and heavily tuned. In real code, reach for the built in sort first.
